All Photos Submit Photo Latest Insights Sizzling Start to September A Hot Summer Send-Off School is back in session, football season has kicked off, and young parking lot maple trees are showing their colors first, as they always do. You would never know it was September if you had awoken from a coma on Wednesday of last week (Sep. 2nd) and walked outside. Many stations across the Southern Appalachian region reached new daily record high temperatures, with all stations posting highs that would be considered "above average" any day of the year, let alone early September. While it is true the start of September is not a traditionally cool time, and Labor Day weekend is quite the busy stretch on beaches and lakes, this heat was anomalous. Nothing Like Last Year The first week of September 2025 was a delight to hot-weather haters! High temperatures were in the vicinity of 15 to 20 degrees cooler than 2026's, with low temperatures dipping into the 40s in Boone on 9/1 and 9/2, 2025. The chart below displays the high and low temperatures (both observed and average) at the Watauga County Hospital station in Boone for September 2025. Now, let's look at the same plot for September 2026, thus far. Notice how high above the faint red average high temperature line Boone got, especially compared to 2025! It wasn't just the High Country that felt fall-like relief last year, either. Hickory had just 3 high temperatures above 80 degrees in the first 7 days of Sept. 2025, whereas this year 6 of 7 were above 80, and 5 of 7 above 90. These numbers aren't remarkably well below normal, but the stark contrast with the deep-frying we experienced last week makes the heat that much harder to stomach. For further comparison, Asheville experienced an average temperature of 68.6F in the first 7 days of Sept. 2025. That was cooler than average by 2.8 degrees, but was only the 28th-coldest first week of September on record there. Meanwhile in 2026, the first 7 days posted an average temperature of 77.1F, nearly 9 degrees warmer than last year, and 5.7 degrees above average. Not to mention, it was the warmest first week of September in the 81 year history of the Asheville Airport weather station. The same can be said for several sites around our area, including Hickory, where the average temperature was at 80.7F for the week. That is most similar to Jacksonville, Florida's climate for early September, and is above average for any 7-day period in Hickory, including mid-July. Crunching Numbers The map above displays where the high temperature for September 3rd, 2026 wound up in the all-time ranking of high temperatures for that date at each site. The 1s indicate that that station experienced its warmest Sept. 3rd high temperature on record, 2s indicate 2nd warmest... and so on. As you can see, there are plenty of 1s, 2s, and 3s. In Boone, high temperatures at the station at the water treatment facility east of downtown reached 84F, 85F, and 86F from the 2nd to the 4th. At our station on top of the office building on Blowing Rock Road, highs reached 89F, 88F, and 89F on the same days. The extra concrete does wonders for high temperatures on the hottest days. Prior to this past week, Boone had not experienced 4 consecutive highs of 85F or greater since 1954. Only 5 total days in every September since 1980 made it to 85F, and in the entire period of record (1929-2025), only 39 total days achieved this. That is just 1.3% of September days in Boone reaching 85 degrees in the last 90+ years. That is a whole bunch of numbers to make the point... it was really, really hot. In Wytheville, highs reached into the 90s 4 consecutive days (Sept. 1-4), but fell just shy of records each day. Those were the first September days above 90 degrees since 2019, raising the total since 2010 to just fifteen September 90s. Summertime Totals The total number of 90 degree days in a year can be a decent measurement for how hot that summer was. There are some details lost in such a simple statistic, but it works as a basic guide. Hickory has logged 37 days at or above 90 degrees in 2026 thus far, which is 6 more days than average (31.2 days). In September, Hickory average just 2.73 days at or above 90F, with the most being 13 in 1954. There have been 5 so far in Sept. 2026. The map below shows the number of 90 degree days for the Southern Appalachians thus far in 2026, through Labor Day. Obviously, the terrain is the main factor in determining who gets 90 and who doesn't. Here is the same map, but zoomed out to show the heat of the North Carolina coastal plain. It is remarkable the variance in climate that one can experience within less than a half day's drive. The worst of the heat has passed, and now we look forward for a real fall feel. Lenoir has yet to dip below 50 degrees this fall. On average, Lenoir's first low temperature in the 40s falls on September 2nd, with the latest wait for 40s pushing into mid-October. There is not any real sign of 2026's wait ending soon, but before you know it, the leaves will change and the winds will blow strong from the northwest once more. Sep 08, 2026 Monday Message for September 7, 2026 It's the Labor Day edition of the Monday Message, available to subscribers. We recap August, and then look forward to a drier and less-hot week after the holiday. Summerlike warmth is not done yet, however. Sep 07, 2026 August 2026 Recap First Weekend Flooding The story all spring and into the beginning of summer had been dry, dry, dry. Drought was just about the only weather story for the first third of summer, but July and August have bucked that trend with gusto. After July ended rather wet, the first weekend of August brought home isolated pockets of 5"+ for a handful of locations across the Ray's Weather coverage region. The most notable pocket of rain was in northeastern Surry County, where 8-10"+ fell on the 1st and 2nd, producing destructive flash flooding in Mount Airy. The city's public works fleet sustained several million dollars worth of damage from the fast-rising floodwaters, and a handful of nearby businesses experienced damage as well. Blowing Rock also saw brief flash flooding that weekend, with training thunderstorms (storms repeatedly moving over the same spot) dropping a localized 5-7 inches of rain while Boone recieved just under 3. No notable damage was reported from the Blowing Rock area, although there was one report of a small amount of water on a ground floor. Wet Summer... For Some Meteorological summer spans the months of June, July, and August, meaning we can now look back on the season as a whole. While temperatures were above normal (but not by a significant margin), precipitation varied by location. This should not come as a surprise, as the vast majority of summertime precipitation comes from afternoon & evening showers & thunderstorms, which are incredibly hit-or-miss. A few miles difference can mean a few inches of rain, which adds up over the course of a summer. Typically, far southwestern North Carolina tends to be the wettest place not only in the state, but in the entire Eastern US. This was not the case this summer, as the maps below show. The first map shows the departure from normal for June 1st to August 31st. Look down near Nantahala National Forest and Brevard, where multiple stations were over 6 inches below average on summer precipitation. Conversely, most stations along and north of Interstate 40 were 2 to 4 inches above average. Highlands, Brevard, Waynesville, and Cullowhee falling shy of Boone's summer total is not something we see often. Highlands recieving less than Asheville is even more surprising, given that Asheville lies in one of the driest areas of the state, the French Broad River Valley, while Highlands lies in a rainforest averaging nearly 90 inches of rain per year. The map below shows total precipitation for the summer. Year-to-date precipitation totals are still behind schedule at all locations in our region... except Marshall in Madison County, which is an inch ahead. Much of Avery County as well as Brevard and Highlands are over 10 inches below what the average year-to-date precipitation should be through the end of August. The Foothills lie 6 to 10 inches behind. Given the El Niño conditions, the late fall and winter period may bring an opportunity to recoup some of that. But, September does not tend to be an especially wet month unless a tropical system moves through, and the tropics have been very quiet thus far. We are approaching the modern record for the deepest run into a year without a storm reaching hurricane strength (the record - Sept. 11th, dating back over 60 years). Looks Like Summer Our monthly bar graph feature for August goes to North Wilkesboro, where temperatures were about where you'd expect them to be in the afternoons. North Wilkesboro did manage to go 31 for 31 on high temperatures at or above 80 degrees (not unusual - the average is 27 days above 80), but only 5 days surpassed 90 degrees, 3 below average. A far cry from last August, which had a remarkable 14 days with high temperatures below 80 degrees. Minimum temperatures were more notably above normal, with 15 lows of 70 or greater and only 1 low below 60 degrees. Temperatures Monthly mean temperatures were above average across the board. The only exceptions on above average lie with a handful of stations that managed below average mean high temperature for the month (Jefferson, Sparta, and Marshall), but low temperatures were above average without exception. Averaging everything out showed generally 1 to 4 degrees above average, again mostly thanks to warm low temperatures. Town by town specifics lie below.
